name: In-Context Autoencoder (ICAE)

paper.title: In-context Autoencoder for Context Compression in a Large Language Model

construction.unit: span of k memory slots (continuous vectors) encoding one context
construction.kept_as: compressed: k = 128 hidden-state vectors per ≤512-token context
construction.processing: LoRA-adapted copy of the LLM reads the context plus k learnable memory tokens; the final hidden states at the memory positions are the slots
construction.writer: ICAE encoder: target LLM + LoRA (query, value) + memory-token embeddings, trained by autoencoding, text continuation and instruction fine-tuning

organization.structure: one fixed-length span per context; long inputs are split into chunks whose spans are concatenated
organization.stores: none beyond the slots, which can be cached for reuse

management.operations: none; slots are produced once per context

retrieval.query: none; the prompt is appended after the slots
retrieval.budget: k = 128 slots for up to 512 tokens (4x); k = 32, 64, 256 also tested

use.context: memory slots followed by the prompt; the original tokens are not given
use.reasoning: single generation by the frozen target LLM

classify.note: A context compressor rather than a searchable store: the decoder always reads every slot, and multi-span inputs only concatenate spans.

stages.ingestion: A context of up to 512 tokens (training maximum) is taken as is; longer inputs are cut into chunks that are compressed one by one (§3.3.3).
stages.construction: k learnable memory tokens are appended to the context and run through the LLM with a LoRA adapter on the query and value projections; the last-layer hidden states at those k positions are the memory slots (k = 128 by default).
stages.organization: One span of slots per context; for long inputs the chunk spans are concatenated in order.
stages.retrieval: No retrieval: the decoder receives every slot.
stages.answer: The untouched target LLM reads the slots followed by the prompt (wrapped in a fine-tuning marker token in the code) and generates the response.
stages.learning: The encoder (LoRA + memory-token embeddings, about 1% extra parameters) is pretrained on the Pile with autoencoding and text continuation, then fine-tuned on 240k PwC (context, prompt, response) triples; the decoder LLM stays frozen.

summary: Compresses a context into 128 memory slots with a LoRA-tuned copy of the LLM, pretrained by autoencoding and continuation so the unchanged LLM can read the slots in place of the original 512 tokens (4x).
notes: Venue: the arXiv v4 PDF header reads 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2024' and the arXiv comment says 'Final camera ready for ICLR'24'; the repo README links OpenReview uREj4ZuGJE. The OpenReview page itself could not be opened (bot challenge), so poster vs spotlight is not recorded. Code: github.com/getao/icae at 469a4688 (2024-05-11). icae_v1 holds the Llama model and fine-tuned inference used in the paper; icae_v2 (Mistral-7B, multi-span, released March-April 2024) is later than the paper's experiments. Text read from the arXiv v4 PDF with pdftotext.

sources.code_note: Latest commit (2024-05-11). code/icae_v1 is the Llama-2-7b-chat release that the README says is used in the paper: model (llama_icae_modeling.py) and fine-tuned inference (ft_inference.py) only, no Llama pretraining script. code/icae_v2 adds Mistral-7B models, multi-span compression up to 5,120 tokens and pretraining/fine-tuning scripts; it post-dates the paper's runs, so it is cited only for the training recipe. The v1 inference example has a typo (memopry_mask, L79) that stops it from running as written.

headline: The memory is 128 continuous vectors per 512-token context, written by a LoRA-tuned copy of the LLM; the LLM that reads them is left unchanged.
Nothing is searched: the decoder reads every slot, so ICAE is a context compressor, not a retrieval memory.
The main quality numbers are GPT-4 pairwise judgements on the authors' own PwC set, not accuracy on an external benchmark.

units.name: Memory span
units.role: the compressed stand-in for one context of up to 512 tokens
units.made_by: ICAE encoder (target LLM + LoRA on q and v, plus memory-token embeddings)

fields.name: memory slots
fields.what: k = 128 last-layer hidden states taken at the memory-token positions; each has the LLM's hidden size

fields.name: original context
fields.what: the input tokens; read only by the encoder and not passed to the decoder

write.how: k learnable memory-token ids are added after the (truncated) context

write.src: paper §3.1; code llama_icae_modeling.py L142-L148, base/modeling_llama_icae.py L306-L308

write.how: the final hidden states at the k memory positions become the memory span
write.out: 128 vectors in place of up to 512 tokens

write.how: a long context is cut into chunks, each compressed separately, and the spans are concatenated; this needs a few multi-span samples in training
write.src: paper §3.3.3, Fig. 6; code icae_v2/modeling_icae_multi_span.py L157-L160, L228-L261

the target LLM with LoRA disabled decodes greedily until end of sequence

includes: memory slots produced by the encoder

compression.what: multi-span memory vs a long context

paper_vs_code.code: v1 (Llama) has no pretraining script; training scripts exist only for the later Mistral v2

open_questions: PwC contexts are about 512 tokens and training stops at 512, so the long-context case rests on perplexity (Fig. 6) rather than a downstream task.
Against the same LLM reading the original context (Table 4), ICAE at k = 128 loses more often than it wins; the Alpaca and StableLM wins compare different models.

glance.a: A span of 128 vectors: the encoder's final hidden states at 128 appended memory tokens, standing in for up to 512 context tokens.
The same LLM with a LoRA adapter on the query and value projections, trained to make the slots useful to the frozen LLM.
No. Every slot goes to the decoder; long inputs become several spans laid side by side.

glance.q: What does the answer model read?
glance.a: The slots, then the prompt. The original text is not given to it.

flow.title: Compress the context
flow.method: LLM + LoRA forward pass over context + 128 memory tokens
flow.model: target LLM (Llama-7b, Llama-2-7b-chat, Llama-2-13b-chat in the paper) + LoRA
flow.sees: The whole context and the memory tokens in one causal pass; the prompt is not seen, so the slots do not depend on the question.

flow.title: Answer
flow.sees: The slots followed by the prompt between [FT] markers; no original text.

text: The context is fed to a LoRA-adapted copy of the LLM with 128 extra memory tokens appended; their final hidden states become the memory slots.
The encoder is pretrained so the frozen LLM can restore or continue the text from the slots, then fine-tuned so it can answer prompts about it.

text: There is no search: the 128 slots are placed in front of the prompt and the unchanged LLM generates the answer from them.
The slots stand in for about 512 context tokens, so the LLM reads a quarter of the input.

ablation.src: paper Table 5 (Llama-2-7b-chat, GPT-4 pairwise judge on PwC test)

discussion.takeaway: An LLM can be taught, with a small LoRA encoder, to squeeze a 512-token context into 128 vectors that the unchanged LLM reads almost as well as the text. Pretraining the encoder by autoencoding is what makes the slots faithful.

claims.claim: The slots keep almost all of the context at 4× compression.
claims.evidence: Autoencoding BLEU 99.1-99.8 and loss below 0.02 for 512 → 128 (Table 6); near-perfect restoration below 300 tokens (Fig. 4).

claims.claim: An LLM reading 128 slots can beat other 7B models reading the full context.
claims.evidence: Llama-7b + ICAE vs Alpaca: win 56.7 / lose 26.9; vs StableLM: 74.1 / 18.8 (Table 4).

claims.claim: Pretraining matters more than slot count.
claims.evidence: Pretrained k=64 roughly matches non-pretrained k=128 (33.1 vs 28.0 win/lose); pretrained vs not at k=128: 60.4 vs 9.5 (Table 5).

claims.claim: Slots are more informative than a natural-language summary of the same length.
claims.evidence: vs a 128-token GPT-4 summary: win 34.1, lose 17.6 (Table 5).
Continuation PPL gap +0.49 / +0.37 / +0.30 for Llama-7b / Llama-2-7b / Llama-2-13b (Table 6).
2.2× to 3.6× lower total latency; over 7× suggested if slots are cached (Table 7, §3.3.2).

limits: Experiments stop at 13B-parameter Llama models because of compute.
Compression is lossy: the compressed model still trails its counterpart with the original context, and going beyond 4× is hard.
The GPT-4 judge favours longer answers, which the authors say understates ICAE's short fine-tuned outputs.
reading: ICAE is working memory for one context: nothing is stored across sessions, searched or updated, and the decoder always reads every slot.
The slots are computed without seeing the prompt, so one span can serve many questions; that is also why they must keep everything rather than what a question needs.
Against the same Llama-2-7b-chat reading the original context, ICAE at k = 128 wins 19.6% and loses 45.4% (Table 4); the large wins are against different models (Alpaca, StableLM).
PwC prompts, reference answers and the judge all come from GPT-4, and training and test contexts are about 512 tokens, so there is no external long-context benchmark in the paper.
The human-like memorisation argument rests on one restoration example (Table 2) and a three-row test on random text (Table 3).

abstract.text: ICAE compresses a long context into a short sequence of memory slots that an LLM can read in place of the original text. The encoder is the same LLM with a small LoRA adapter and a set of memory tokens whose final hidden states become the slots; the LLM that reads them is left unchanged. The encoder is pretrained on large text corpora to reconstruct and continue the input from the slots, then fine-tuned on context-prompt-response data. With Llama models it reaches 4x compression with small quality loss, faster inference and lower GPU memory, and the authors relate the slots to human working memory.
